title: Garage Door Prototype: Owning the MQTT Integration Boundary
summary: In a five-person IoT capstone, I owned the MQTT communication layer and later shared Android-side implementation where it intersected with messaging, location, and device control. The prototype connected a mobile app through Mosquitto to a Raspberry Pi that triggered the existing garage-door remote signal.

paragraphs: The project explored a phone-based alternative to a dedicated garage-door remote, supporting manual commands and a proximity-triggered opening concept.

This was a five-person graduation project. My primary responsibility was the MQTT communication layer: setting up and testing Mosquitto, defining the message flow, and coordinating the boundaries that connected the mobile app to the device side.

The Android app began as another teammate's responsibility. As integration work expanded, we divided the remaining implementation, and I contributed to messaging, location, and device-control paths that crossed the MQTT boundary.

content.title: My responsibility was communication and integration
content.body: I owned MQTT and contributed to the related Android paths. The Raspberry Pi bridge, web dashboard, database, enclosure, and the complete prototype were team work or teammate-owned—not features I claim as solely mine.

sections.title: Use MQTT as the integration boundary

paragraphs: Mosquitto separated message routing from physical door control. The Android client published an intent; the broker routed it; the Raspberry Pi-side controller interpreted it and acted.

The documented flow included CreateUser, ControlMessage, and DeviceState topics. Control payloads used forms such as open/{android_id} and close/{android_id}, allowing the device side to associate a command with an Android client.
Manual controls and the proximity workflow published into the same downstream control path. Device-state messages returned through MQTT so the Android application could update its view of the system.

nodes.label: Android app
nodes.responsibility: Creates manual or proximity-based control intent and displays returned state.

nodes.label: Mosquitto broker
nodes.responsibility: Routes published commands and device-state messages between clients.

nodes.label: Raspberry Pi bridge
nodes.responsibility: Interprets the routed command and triggers the remote-control signal.

nodes.label: Existing door remote
nodes.responsibility: Sends the signal understood by the garage-door receiver.

nodes.label: Garage-door receiver
nodes.responsibility: Receives the existing remote signal and operates the door.

content.title: The broker routes; the controller acts
content.body: MQTT did not operate the door directly. It provided the asynchronous communication boundary; the Raspberry Pi-side implementation owned interpretation and physical actuation.

sections.title: Connect location intent to the existing remote signal

paragraphs: The Android flow stored a home location and distance setting, compared them with the phone's current GPS position, and published a control command when the configured proximity condition was met.

In the demonstrated setup, a Raspberry Pi placed near the garage-door receiver triggered the existing remote-control signal. That hardware bridge was essential to the team prototype, but it was not my implementation responsibility.
A phone-accessible server configuration dashboard was explored but remained incomplete. It is excluded from the finished feature story rather than presented as delivered functionality.

content.title: A demonstrated integration path, not a deployable product
content.body: The team demonstrated an end-to-end path from Android intent to the existing door remote. The evidence supports a working prototype concept, not production claims about safety, security, reliability, or GPS accuracy.

sections.title: Recognize what a real deployment would require

content.title: Prototype implementation versus a redesign today

sides.label: Capstone prototype
sides.summary: A student-built integration that proved the cross-device concept.

sides.label: Redesign today
sides.summary: A safer, more explicit system with production boundaries.

values.prototype: Java application with messaging, location, and device-control work divided across teammates.
values.redesign: Kotlin with clearer separation between UI state, location policy, MQTT transport, and command orchestration.

values.prototype: A configured GPS distance threshold could publish a control command.
values.redesign: Treat accuracy, boundary jitter, background execution, user confirmation, and fail-safe behavior as explicit states.

values.prototype: A Raspberry Pi triggered the existing remote-control signal.
values.redesign: Integrate at the controller level with sensors, interlocks, diagnostics, and a defined fail-safe path.

values.prototype: The planned configuration dashboard remained incomplete.
values.redesign: Provide configuration, status history, diagnostics, and access boundaries as a maintained product surface.

content.title: The useful result is the boundary, not the polish
content.body: Much of the implementation could be refactored today. The durable lesson was learning to identify who owns commands, device state, transport, and physical action—a responsibility boundary I now apply to frontend state and component design.
